Record visitors, version 1
==========================

Optional record contracts are checked against ordinary C declarations:

  cesta record-visitor --schema frame.records -o frame_visit.h \
    --cc gcc -std=c11 frame.h

The input remains the real C header or translation unit, with its actual
typedefs and compiler configuration. The command elaborates declarations,
not function bodies. It never invokes Lean or another proof assistant.
No visitor framework or allocation ledger is linked into the program.

  (cesta record-visitors/1
    (owner atoms)
    (owner episode)
    (visitor move
      (owner atoms) (type "Atom *") (call move_atom_slot)
      (argument address) (effects write)
      (obligation "Moves a shared atom through the collector's forwarding map;
                   updates the borrowed slot and retains no frame/context."))
    (record "Frame"
      (function frame_visit) (context "Collector") (receiver write)
      (field value (borrow read nullable) (owner atoms) (visit move))
      (field episode (borrow read) (owner episode)
        (keep "Lifetime carrier outside the collected semispace."))
      (field revision value)))

Each actual C field must occur exactly once. Pointer-bearing fields, including
arrays and inline records containing references, need borrow/owns, an owner
role, and either a visitor or an explicit keep obligation. A value field
contains no pointers. Owner roles are nominal, author-supplied lifetime domains;
the generator checks their agreement with the selected native policy. They
do not infer which runtime arena produced an arbitrary legacy C pointer.
This is separate from Cesta's existing function-level ownership admission.

Borrow access applies to the referent. A write visitor taking a field by value
needs write borrowing. Passing a field's address updates the record's slot and
requires a write receiver. Owning fields retain their release authority;
mutating their ownership requires a separately specified transfer and is refused
here. A GC edge therefore does not imply unique ownership.

A function policy names an actual nonvariadic bool function with two parameters:
context pointer and field argument. A counted policy has a third size_t count.
The generator checks the real prototype. A macro policy uses (macro NAME) in
place of (call NAME); its interface is (CONTEXT, ARGUMENT, FAIL), or
(CONTEXT, ARGUMENT, COUNT, FAIL) when counted. Its meaning remains a named native
obligation. Types use existing C typedefs/tags, standard scalar spellings and
pointer qualifiers. Name complex array/function types by a real C typedef.

The record can emit (macro NAME) instead of (function NAME). This supports
collector declaration headers whose types and policy macros become visible
only where the arm is expanded. Macro arguments must be side-effect free;
failure is a caller-provided transfer such as goto failed. Standard C11 type
and layout assertions check the receiver, context and fields when expanded.
Function visitors are ordinary static inline C functions. Include the actual
declarations and policy interfaces before the generated function header.

(when FLAG) skips a visitor when an ordinary integer/bool field is false.
(count LENGTH) requires a counted visitor and an ordinary unsigned count field.
Before visiting any fields, generated guards check nonempty null buffers,
count-to-byte overflow, and fixed-array bounds. Zero counts visit no elements.
The caller still supplies the actual backing extent for pointer buffers.

Native policies own relocation, forwarding, weak/ephemeron behavior and commit
semantics. A failed visitor may leave a visited prefix updated. The caller must
retain the relevant storage or perform its own rollback. Generated field
coverage is not a proof of a complete root inventory or of collector behavior.

Generation validates the complete module before replacing an output. Each
requested output is published atomically; generation refusal preserves it.
Source/schema files and coincident code/facts outputs cannot be overwritten.
Regenerate when a header, schema, target or compiler configuration changes.

--facts FILE writes declaration/contract metadata for development audits and
models. It is never required to generate, build, link or run a program. The
development Lean models concern these added contracts; Cesta users need no
Lean installation, proof library or proof receipt. Headers retain native C ABI.

Maintainers can replay the declaration and relative region-effect models with
tests/developer_record_models.py --facts FILE --lean-project PROJECT. This is a
separate development command, absent from product builds and ordinary tests.
It checks field coverage, nominal owner agreement and access rights against the
emitted declarations, with altered-declaration refusals. Native allocation
provenance, traversal behavior and the generated C execution remain distinct
obligations.
